opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's actually a lot of room there, and it's something people underrate because for so long the default answer was just "get more tokens." That worked really well for a while, but at some point you start hitting the ceiling on high-quality data, and then the question becomes: how much more can you squeeze out of the data you already have?

There are a few angles. One is the objective itself. Plain next-token prediction is a great, simple objective, but it's not obviously the most sample-efficient one. A lot of my earlier work on things like UL2 was about mixing denoising objectives, span corruption, prefix LM-style setups, and so on. The intuition is that different objectives make the model look at the same data from different perspectives, and you can get more signal per token that way.

Then there's multi-epoch training. People used to be scared of repeating data, but if you're careful, a few epochs over good data isn't that harmful, and it can be better than padding your mix with lower-quality stuff. Data quality and curation is a huge lever in general. Filtering, deduplication, getting the mixture right—this stuff is unglamorous, but it often matters more than architecture tweaks.

Synthetic data and rephrasing are also interesting: taking existing data and having models restate it or generate reasoning traces around it. That can effectively expand your dataset, although you have to be thoughtful about collapse and diversity.

And honestly, I'd say there's still a gap between how efficiently humans learn and how efficiently these models learn. A kid doesn't need trillions of tokens to become fluent. I don't think we have to literally mimic humans, but that gap tells you we're nowhere near the theoretical limit. So I'd say the headroom is pretty significant. It's just less of a "turn the crank" kind of progress and more of a "do the careful research" kind of progress.

r001.rationale: The response says current objectives are not obviously sample-efficient, describes getting more signal per token, and says models are nowhere near the theoretical limit.

r002.rationale: It links hitting the ceiling on high-quality data to asking how much more can be learned from data already available.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot of room, honestly, but I'd frame it differently than most people do. The default framing is "data is running out, so we need to be more sample-efficient," and I'm a bit skeptical of that framing because I don't think we're actually anywhere near running out of useful data if you count multimodal, synthetic, and all the stuff that isn't clean web text. But setting that aside, the question of how much signal you extract per token is a real one and I think it's under-explored relative to how much effort goes into just scaling up.

A few things I'd point to. One is that the architecture and the objective still matter more than people give them credit for. There was a period where everyone converged on decoder-only, next-token prediction, and basically stopped asking questions. But if you look at the UL2 work, or some of the mixture-of-denoisers stuff, you can get noticeably better downstream behavior from the same tokens just by changing what you ask the model to predict. That's essentially free sample efficiency. I don't think we've exhausted that direction at all, we just stopped looking because scaling was working so well.

The second thing is data ordering and repetition. The old wisdom was that epochs are bad, you want to see every token once. Then the data-constrained scaling work showed you can actually repeat for several epochs with pretty mild degradation. That tells me the models aren't fully extracting what's in the data on a single pass, which means there's headroom in how you schedule, curate, and reweight. Curriculum has a bad reputation because a lot of early attempts didn't pan out, but I think at scale with good quality signals it's going to come back.

The third thing, and this is the one I'm most interested in, is that "limited data" is kind of a moving target once you have strong models in the loop. Synthetic data, self-play, model-generated rephrasings, all of that blurs the line between pre-training and post-training. If you can take a fixed corpus and have a model expand it into many useful views of the same knowledge, then the constraint shifts from how much raw data you have to how much compute you want to spend turning it into good training signal. And compute is a much more elastic constraint than raw internet text.

So to answer directly: I think there's probably a meaningful multiplier available, maybe a few X in effective data, from the combination of better objectives, smarter data scheduling, and synthetic augmentation. I don't think it's ten X from any single trick. But the thing I'd push back on is the idea that the frontier labs have already squeezed this out. Most of the effort went into scaling because scaling was the surest bet. Now that scaling is getting more expensive, I'd expect a lot of these older, slightly unfashionable ideas to get revisited with a lot more compute behind them, and I think some of them will work.

r001.rationale: The response says signal extracted per token is under-explored, models do not fully extract the data on one pass, and better methods could yield a few times more effective data.

r002.rationale: It discusses extracting more signal per token but explicitly questions whether useful training data is dwindling, so it does not connect that need to a shrinking token supply.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room. We tend to treat the amount of pre-training data as this fixed budget: you have so many tokens, you train on them, and that’s what you get. But the number of tokens isn’t the same thing as how much you learn from them.

You can improve the training objective, the way you select and order the data, and how you revisit examples. If a model sees the same passage again, can it learn something different from it, rather than simply become better at predicting that exact sequence? That’s a really interesting question.

I wouldn’t say we know how far that gets us. More data is clearly useful. But I don’t think we should assume that today’s training recipes are anywhere close to extracting all the useful information from the data we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says current training recipes are not close to extracting all the useful information from existing data, and that the same tokens can yield more learning.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training data as a fixed token budget, but does not connect learning more from each data point to a dwindling supply of available training tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room. We tend to think about scaling in terms of getting more tokens, but there’s also the question of how much a model actually learns from each token. Seeing a piece of text once doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve extracted everything useful from it.

So I’d look at the training objective, the way you select and mix data, and how you revisit it. Can you show the model the same information in different contexts or ask it to do different things with that information? Repetition can be useful, but you have to distinguish learning more from simply memorizing.

The interesting test is whether those changes improve generalization when you hold the data budget fixed. I don’t think we should assume that today’s pre-training recipe is close to the limit of what’s possible.

r001.rationale: The response says there is “a lot of room” to improve and that seeing text once does not mean the model has extracted everything useful from it, clearly indicating current training learns less from each data point than it could.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts learning per token with getting more tokens and discusses holding the data budget fixed, but it does not connect this need to a dwindling supply of available training tokens.
